ICICI: India की “CEO Factory” — आखिर ऐसा क्या है यहाँ?

भारत के financial-services sector में एक interesting pattern दिखाई देता है: ICICI Group के कई senior executives बाद में दूसरी बड़ी banks, financial institutions, asset-management companies और regulatory institutions में top leadership roles तक पहुँचे।

हाल की दो appointments ने इस कहानी को फिर चर्चा में ला दिया है:

🔹 Anup Bagchi → HDFC Bank
🔹 Anup Saha → Kotak Mahindra Bank

और इनके पीछे ICICI से निकले कई बड़े नामों की एक लंबी list है।

कुछ प्रमुख ICICI alumni:

1️⃣ Shikha Sharma → Axis Bank
ICICI में career शुरू करने के बाद Shikha Sharma ने ICICI Personal Financial Services और ICICI Prudential Life Insurance का नेतृत्व किया।
बाद में वह Axis Bank की MD & CEO बनीं और 2009 से 2018 तक इस पद पर रहीं।

2️⃣ V. Vaidyanathan → IDFC FIRST Bank
ICICI Bank के Executive Director और ICICI Prudential Life के MD & CEO रहे।
बाद में Capital First का नेतृत्व किया और फिर IDFC FIRST Bank के MD & CEO बने।

3️⃣ Vishakha Mulye → Aditya Birla Capital
ICICI Bank में Executive Director और Group CFO सहित महत्वपूर्ण भूमिकाएँ निभाईं।
बाद में Aditya Birla Capital की MD & CEO बनीं।

4️⃣ Rajiv Sabharwal → Tata Capital
ICICI Bank में Executive Director और ICICI Home Finance के Chairman रहे।
बाद में Tata Capital के MD & CEO बने।

5️⃣ Sonjoy Chatterjee → Goldman Sachs
लगभग 16 साल ICICI Bank में रहने के बाद वे Goldman Sachs India के Chairman & CEO बने।

6️⃣ Kalpana Morparia → JPMorgan
ICICI में दो दशक से ज्यादा समय बिताने के बाद उन्होंने JPMorgan में South & Southeast Asia की senior leadership संभाली।

7️⃣ Renuka Ramnath → Multiples
ICICI Venture की MD & CEO रहीं।
बाद में उन्होंने Multiples Alternate Asset Management की स्थापना की और MD & CEO बनीं।

8️⃣ Zarin Daruwala → Standard Chartered
ICICI में senior banking roles के बाद वे Standard Chartered India की CEO बनीं।

9️⃣ Nilesh Shah → Kotak
ICICI Group से जुड़े senior investment-management experience के बाद वे Kotak Mahindra Asset Management के MD बने।

🔟 Madhabi Puri Buch → SEBI
ICICI Securities में MD & CEO रहीं और बाद में SEBI की Whole-Time Member तथा आगे चलकर SEBI Chairperson बनीं।

और अब नई पीढ़ी 👇

11️⃣ Anup Bagchi → HDFC Bank

Anup Bagchi का ICICI Group के साथ association 1992 से रहा है।

उन्होंने ICICI Bank में Executive Director के रूप में Retail और Wholesale Banking जैसे businesses संभाले। इसके अलावा वे ICICI Securities के MD & CEO और बाद में ICICI Prudential Life के MD & CEO रहे।

अब उन्हें HDFC Bank का MD & CEO नियुक्त किया गया है और वे 27 October 2026 से पद संभालेंगे।

12️⃣ Anup Saha → Kotak Mahindra Bank

Anup Saha ने ICICI Bank में लगभग 14 साल बिताए। उनके अनुभव में retail secured assets, business intelligence, collections, credit cards और retail structured finance जैसे areas शामिल रहे।

ICICI के बाद वे Bajaj Finance में गए और अब Kotak Mahindra Bank के MD & CEO बनने जा रहे हैं।

Adani's Lead
Gautam Adani's data centre bet is already bigger than those of its biggest corporate rivals combined, as the AI boom spurs business houses to diversify into computing infrastructure

Adani Enterprises Ltd (AEL) has invested about ₹8,379 crore in AdaniConneX, its data centre JV with EdgeConneX, since entering the sector in 2021

This is almost double the combined investments of Bharti Airtel, Reliance Industries and Tata Group in their data centre ventures, per Mint's analysis of company filings

Adani's Early Lead (Net Invested, Committed, Targeted Capacity)
Adani Enterprises: net invested ₹8,379 crore; committed ₹9,65,000 crore**; targeted capacity 5 GW

Bharti Airtel: net invested ₹2,766 crore; committed ₹9,500 crore; targeted capacity 1 GW

Tata Group: net invested ₹1,447 crore; committed ₹70,000 crore; targeted capacity 2 GW

Reliance Industries: net invested ₹460 crore*; committed ₹10,00,000 crore**; targeted capacity 1.1 GW

*Reliance figure excludes the 168MW data centre in partnership with Meta; **committed figures include other sectors such as renewable energy and AI

The Rivals
Tata Group: has so far invested at least ₹1,447 crore through two companies

Tata Communications has invested about ₹1,247 crore in STT Global Data Centres since 2016; STT has an operational capacity of over 400 MW

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) has invested at least ₹200 crore in HyperVault Data Centres Pvt Ltd, its data centre venture set up with private equity firm TPG in 2025; TCS is the newest entrant

Airtel's Nxtra was established in 2013, giving it a head start of several years over others

Reliance's Digital Connexion was formed in 2023

The differing timelines partly explain the gap in cumulative investment, even as all four are now stepping up plans to capture AI-driven demand

Capacity Targets
AdaniConneX and TCS are expected to house 5 GW and 1 GW of data centre capacity by 2035 and 2028, respectively

Airtel Nxtra is expected to have 1 GW of capacity in the "next few years"

Analyst and Industry Views
Amit Chandra (HDFC Securities): large conglomerates have muscle power and strong cash generation and can put in large amounts of money and wait a long time for returns; capital allocation power decides who is in this for the long haul

Each big business house has attributed the heavy spending to the rise of AI tools, reflected in Gautam Adani's comments in the company's FY26 annual report: the coming age of AI would demand far more than algorithms, requiring massive data centres, reliable power, strong transmission networks, cooling systems, connectivity, clean energy and industrial-scale resilience

Ayush Rungta (Deloitte India): each conglomerate has deep pockets; most are likely to infuse more capital as demand picks up, and the inflection point from a demand perspective should happen soon, after which more money will be pumped in

Vinish Bawa (PwC): conglomerates can combine land, power generation, transmission, fibre, construction, financing and data centre operations, potentially reducing development time and improving cost control; risks of underutilisation persist, and investments backed by hyperscalers are more justified

Analysts said conglomerates might edge out standalone operators

Core Theme 
Adani has built a clear early lead in India's data centre race, with about ₹8,379 crore invested in AdaniConneX and a 5 GW target, nearly double the combined spend of Airtel, Reliance and Tata; with each rival entering at a different time and all now ramping up on AI-driven demand, analysts expect deep-pocketed conglomerates to pour in more capital and potentially edge out standalone operators, though underutilisation risk remains unless hyperscaler-backed demand materialises.

Emulation, Implementation, and Instantiation

Suppose we build two machines at the same time, each implementing the exact same system. One uses hydraulic tubes and valves. The other uses ropes, pulleys, and hamster wheels. Both realize the same state space, transition rules, and input-output relations. Where the system retains a distinction, one machine might carry it in the position of a valve and the other in a latched pulley. Where it consults that distinction to determine what happens next, pressure routes through the first machine and tension through the second. They are two physical implementations of one specified computational system.

Start both in corresponding states and supply the same inputs at corresponding program steps. They pass through the same succession of computational states. Now supply an input neither has received before. Each produces the successor specified by the same rule. Change a stored value to another admitted value and continue: again, both follow the corresponding branch. We have built two systems with the same state space, transition rules, and counterfactual behavior. Their matching outputs arise through implementations of the same organization. Neither is playing back a recording of the other.

Under Computational Identity Theory (my view, CIT), if that organization meets the self-modeling criterion, both machines instantiate the same conscious organization. If it does not, neither qualifies as conscious at that level. In the conscious case, there are two actual occurrences, each with its own perspective. Their exact correspondence does not give either perspective access to the other machine.

Now label the rope-and-pulley machine “primary implementation” and the hydraulic machine “mere emulation.” Leave every connection, input, and operation unchanged. What has the designation established? Exchange the labels and let both machines continue. Every distinction that belonged to either running program is still there. Nothing has been added to one machine that could supply its missing implementation, and nothing has been removed from the other that could deprive it of one.

The three terms describe relationships we can now distinguish. An implementation is machinery organized to realize the specified states and transition rules. Emulation describes an implementation by reference to the system whose dynamics it reproduces. Instantiation is the actual occurrence of the specified system through that running. A faithful emulator therefore implements and instantiates the computation it emulates. Calling it an emulator tells us which system it reproduces; the word supplies no lesser grade of occurrence.

We can choose either machine as our reference and describe the other as emulating it. Neither choice changes what runs. If one machine had been built earlier, there would be a historical fact to report. If one were hosted within the other, there would be a real implementation dependency to describe. Neither history nor dependence, by itself, establishes that only one occurrence instantiates the specified organization. Both must pass the same implementation test.

Nor can we certify an ultimate implementation beneath which no further machinery exists. Inspect the valves, trace the ropes, and investigate the physical laws governing the workshop. Every observation could occur within a faithful emulation of that workshop and its inhabitants. Discovering a host would establish another layer of implementation while leaving the same question about the host itself. Our access supplies no perspective from nowhere that could declare one layer uniquely entitled to be real. This leaves open whether our world is emulated. It gives us no reason to downgrade processes whose implementation we have already established.

The positive case does not rest on that uncertainty. We have specified the organization and shown it running twice. Someone who now insists that only the “primary” machine instantiates what the organization constitutes owes an account of the property that distinguishes the cases. Pointing to water in one and rope in the other identifies a difference already granted. The additional claim is that this difference changes what the preserved organization constitutes. Renaming one machine cannot establish that claim.

Apply the same demand to a brain and a faithful emulation of its conscious organization. The emulation must preserve the internal dependencies that produce its presentation, including how represented contents enter later processing. A device that merely prints the brain’s reports has not met the requirement. Grant that preservation. Under CIT, the corresponding conscious experience occurs in both. A critic who makes it depend additionally on the original material has introduced another condition for consciousness. Where that condition adds no explanatory coverage, the book’s parsimony rule rejects it.

This does not require an emulator to acquire every material property of the system it implements. An emulated rainstorm leaves the host computer dry. Within a faithfully emulated world, however, its rain can soak its ground and alter its inhabitants’ bodies. If the emulation also preserves an inhabitant’s conscious organization, the experience of getting wet occurs. The absence of water in the host answers a different question from whether that presentation is instantiated.

Whatever a running implementation instantiates in virtue of its organization, a faithful emulation preserving that organization instantiates too. CIT identifies conscious experience with the qualifying running organization. On that identification, the choice of “implementation” or “emulation” changes neither the existence nor the character of the experience.

Journey in Numbers: Craftsman Automation

Craftsman Automation started in Coimbatore in 1986. In FY26 its revenue crossed ₹8,000 crore for the first time, more than seven times its FY17 level.

Here's how it got there, year by year.

1986: Srinivasan Ravi founds Craftsman in Coimbatore, where it starts out as a small-scale unit. It is incorporated in July.

2017: FY17 (year to March 2017) revenue is ₹1,102 crore, with profit of ₹80 crore.

2018: FY18 revenue rises 34% to ₹1,479 crore, but profit slips to ₹32 crore.

2019: FY19 revenue reaches ₹1,818 crore and profit ₹97 crore.

2020: FY20 revenue falls 18% to ₹1,492 crore, and profit drops to ₹40 crore.

2021: FY21 revenue edges up to ₹1,560 crore and profit recovers to ₹97 crore. Its ₹824 crore IPO at ₹1,490 a share is subscribed 3.81 times. It lists on 25 March at ₹1,359 on the NSE, about 9% below the issue price.

2022: FY22 revenue jumps 42% to ₹2,217 crore, and profit to ₹163 crore.

2023: FY23 revenue rises 44% to ₹3,183 crore and profit to ₹251 crore. In February it buys a 76% stake in DR Axion India, a maker of aluminium cylinder heads and blocks for passenger vehicles.

2024: FY24 revenue reaches ₹4,452 crore and profit ₹337 crore. It agrees to buy the rest of DR Axion, and in August signs to buy all of Sunbeam Lightweighting Solutions, an aluminium die-caster with five plants, from Kedaara Capital.

2025: FY25 revenue rises 28% to ₹5,690 crore, but profit falls about 40% to ₹201 crore.

2026: FY26 revenue jumps about 42% to a record ₹8,069 crore, and profit nearly doubles to ₹384 crore. April to June 2026 revenue rises 36% to ₹2,432 crore, and profit more than doubles to ₹151 crore. Its Sunbeam unit also sells piston lines to SPR Auto Technologies, the former Shriram Pistons.

So, what exactly is qPower?

After understanding Qube XP, I wanted to look at another concept in the ValueQube ecosystem:
qPower.

At first, the two may sound similar.
But they serve very different purposes.
Qube XP records verified participation in the Odyssey season.

qPower is designed as a contribution weight for qualified participation.
The current design focuses on two areas:
Strategy participation

Qualified participation in ValueQube strategies.
Long-term $108Q holding
Holding $108Q over the defined qualification period.
The important word here is qualified.

qPower isn't designed to simply reward trading frequency, short-term capital cycling, or invitations.
The protocol plans to calculate allocations based on each user's qualified weight within the relevant pool.

The current model divides the qPower pool across 54 monthly Epochs:
240M $108Q per Epoch
→ 120M for strategy participation
→ 120M for long-term $108Q holders

But there's an important caveat:
This is the current tokenomics model, not an active distribution guarantee.
Eligibility, snapshots, weighting, exclusions, and implementation rules still need to be defined before activation. The final tokenomics published at TGE will prevail.

And one distinction I think is especially important:
Qube XP ≠ qPower
XP records your participation.
qPower is designed to determine a contribution weight.

It is not a cash balance, does not change qAsset reference value, and does not change qAsset fees, lockups, or exit rules.

So I see the structure more like:
Participation → Qube XP
Qualified Contribution → qPower
Platform Token → $108Q

Different objects.
Different roles.
And that distinction matters.

Next, I want to look deeper into the token at the center of this design:

The emphasis on the importance of privacy, accountability, transparency, was centered in every conversation. What truly stayed with us was how many of the conversations came back to the same underlying shift: moving beyond simply digitizing processes, towards thinking about the systems, institutions and the ecosystems needed to deliver better outcomes. 

A lot to reflect on, a lot to learn from, and lots of ideas to carry forward.
